citation.title: “Carbon Bombs” - Mapping key fossil fuel projects
citation.type: journal article, published version (open access, CC BY; available online 12 May 2022; 10 pages)

question: Which are the biggest fossil fuel extraction projects worldwide (called carbon bombs), where are they, how large are their potential emissions, and what is their status.
data: Project-level reserve data: Rystad UCube (oil and gas, 2020), BP Statistical Review of Energy, US EIA coal reserve sources and Global Energy Monitor's Global Coal Mine Tracker (coal, 2020-2021). Production data from Rystad and the German BGR. Result: 425 projects (230 coal mines, 195 oil and gas projects). The full project list is in supplementary Appendix 1 and 2, which are not in the extracted text.
method: Screen reserve databases for extraction projects above a reserve threshold, convert reserves to potential CO2 using average IPCC emission factors, keep projects above 1 gigaton CO2. Only extraction projects are counted. A simple scenario ('harvest mode', extraction continues without new investment) is run for projects already producing. No company-level or organisation-level classification is done.

definitions.definition: A proposed or existing fossil fuel extraction project (coal mine, oil or gas project) whose complete extraction and burning would emit more than 1 gigaton of CO2.
definitions.quote: a proposed or existing fossil fuel extraction project (a coal mine, oil or gas project) that would result in more than 1 gigaton of CO2 emissions

definitions.definition: Taken from the Rystad database: a practical aggregation of assets developed as one industry project.
definitions.quote: Typically a Project consists of assets to be developed as one industry project.

definitions.definition: Recoverable reserves: coal at a mine considered economically mineable with the highest degree of confidence; where unavailable, resources were used and flagged.
definitions.quote: the amount of coal at a mine that is considered economically mineable with the highest degree of confidence

definitions.definition: Only extraction projects; transport infrastructure and demand-side infrastructure such as power plants are excluded, to avoid double counting.
definitions.quote: We only include extraction projects, but not transport infrastructure (LNG terminals, pipelines, ports)

definitions.definition: Emissions if all reserves were burnt; no adjustment for methane leakage or non-energy uses.
definitions.quote: Our numbers are therefore labeled as potential emissions - the emissions that would result if all reserves were burnt.

proxies.indicator: Rystad UCube project with more than 2.5 billion barrels of oil equivalent or 400 bcm of gas equivalent reserves, then kept only if potential emissions are at least 1 Gt CO2.
proxies.quote: identified all projects, existing and planned, with more than 2.5 billion barrels of oil equivalent reserves or 400 bcm of gas equivalent reserves.

proxies.indicator: Countries with more than 375 million tons of reserves in BP Statistical Review first, then individual mines above type-specific reserve thresholds (385 to 835 mt depending on coal type; Table 1).
proxies.quote: identified all countries over a threshold of 375 million tons of coal reserves in the BP Statistical Review of Energy

proxies.indicator: Reserves multiplied by average IPCC emission factors for direct CO2 from burning.
proxies.quote: we use average IPCC emissions factors for direct CO2 emissions from burning the fossil fuels in question

proxies.concept: company exposure to stranded assets (mentioned, not used)
proxies.indicator: Stranded-asset analyses flag the companies and projects most exposed for investors; the paper describes this as a complement to its own approach.
proxies.quote: These analyses help flag the companies and projects most exposed to potential asset stranding for investors.

findings.claim: 425 carbon bombs identified: 195 oil and gas, 230 coal.
findings.quote: We have identified 425 carbon bombs. 195 oil and gas projects fall into this category

findings.claim: Carbon bombs are concentrated in a few countries; China has the most.
findings.quote: There are only 10 countries with more than 10 carbon bombs: China (141), Russia (41), United States (28), Iran (24)

findings.claim: Carbon bombs already operating account for a large share of 2019 global production.
findings.quote: carbon bomb projects in operation were responsible for 45% of global oil and gas production and 25% of global coal production in 2019

findings.claim: State-owned enterprises are named as among the energy companies planning additional extraction projects (stated in the introduction, not measured).
findings.quote: are still being planned by energy companies, including state-owned enterprises (SOEs).

findings.claim: An existing public list of company fossil fuel reserves (Carbon Underground 200) does not cover most SOEs.
findings.quote: which however does not cover most SOEs.

limitations.point: Oil and gas data came from a commercial paid database; coal data are hard to bring to a common standard.
limitations.quote: for oil and gas we had to resort to a commercial, paid service (Rystad) to get reliable data with global coverage.

limitations.point: Some projects may be missed (exploration still under way) and the list changes with prices.
limitations.quote: Some existing carbon bombs may have escaped our method where exploration activities are still taking place.

limitations.point: Emissions are potential, not forecast, and the method is deliberately simple.
limitations.quote: Our numbers are therefore labeled as potential emissions - the emissions that would result if all reserves were burnt.

limitations.point: The paper works at project level and names no operating companies in the text read; the project list is only in supplementary appendices that are not in this file. It cannot by itself identify fossil fuel-linked organisations.
The extracted metadata lists only one author and has a garbled title; the author list above comes from page 1 text. No instructions addressed to a reader or an AI were found.
